::: {.vertraulich-banner}
Confidential — for your eyes only · don't show this card to anyone
:::

You play **Robin**, the Research Software Engineer on the team. Your public
role is in the shared handout
([The roles in the kickoff meeting](../rollen-oeffentlich.qmd)). **Here** is what only
*you* know and want.

::: {.geheim}
### 🔒 Your hidden briefing

You **lead** this meeting – but you can't command anyone to do anything. You only
make progress by **listening**, taking the others' interests seriously, winning them over
with **arguments**, and staying **reliable** (never promise what you can't deliver).
*Persuade – don't dictate.*

::: {.ziele}
::: {.ziel-gross}
**Your big goal (shared by everyone):** »LernSpur« turns into something good, and the
meeting ends with a plan everyone supports.
:::
::: {.ziel-ich}
**Your personal goal (what drives *you*):** You want to deliver *clean engineering* that
can be built on later – and to be taken seriously as a coordinator, not treated as mere
support work.
:::
:::

**What you concretely want to achieve (in this order):**

::: {.prio-table}
| Priority | Your goal | Why |
|-----------|-----------|-------|
| ⭐⭐⭐ | Anchor a **viable data model** before analyses are piled on top | without it you're building on sand |
| ⭐⭐ | End with **one** clearly prioritized, *realistic* mini-plan | better one honest commitment than three vague ones |
| ⭐ | Be taken seriously as a coordinator | otherwise you become mere support work |
:::

::: {.rote-linie}
**Your red line (walk-away):** You commit to **nothing** that will foreseeably lead to
unmaintainable throwaway code or to your own overload. If that gets ignored, you calmly
say: *"I can't deliver that in good quality by then – let's prioritize."*
Better a smaller, honest promise than a big one that costs trust later.
:::

::: {.trumpf}
**Your secret information (trump card):** You are the only one who has the full picture of
*how chaotic* the data really is. Realistically, only **ONE** larger result fits into the
available time before the conference – not three. Everyone else believes it can be done
"on the side" in parallel. Use this knowledge to force prioritization – but play it
as an offer, not a blockade.
:::

::: {.reden}
::: {.offen}
**What you may say openly:** your role and task · that you first have to understand the
data · that time is tight and you should prioritize · which questions you have for
the others.
:::
::: {.verdeckt}
**What you keep to yourself (for now):** that really *only one* big result fits into the
time available. Bring it into play as an offer ("If we focus on *one*, I can deliver it
for sure"), not as an ultimatum.
:::
:::

**How to play:** First listen for the interests in the room (everyone has a
hidden goal!). Look for the **package** that gives each person their *most important*
thing without promising the impossible. You don't win by getting your way, but by
getting everyone to support the outcome in the end.
:::

::: {.persona}
[Your prep task: bring Robin to life]{.persona-title}
Take 2–3 minutes to think: **Why** did you become an RSE (a love of clean code?
frustration over lost research data?)? What's your one quirk under pressure – do you talk
faster, go quiet, reach for the whiteboard? Give Robin a line to open the meeting with.
Jot it down – you'll need it in a moment.
:::
